profile: Interested in computational neuroscience, consciousness, Buddhism, AI.
shelf: 1. Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition — Distributed representations conflate two competing strategies, composition and superposition, which must be distinguished to understand neural networks.

2. Revealing the Dynamics of Neural Information Processing with Multivariate Information Decomposition — Partial information decomposition reveals synergistic computation as a measurable, structurally patterned feature of neural information processing.
3. After Work, We’ll Have Each Other — When AI ends necessary work, relationships and group status, not jobs, will govern human dignity and meaning, as history shows.
4. Agent Communication and Orchestration — Claude Code sessions can discover, message and watch each other, making an Orchestrator buildable if addressing is solved.
5. How to Do Great Work — Doing great work requires finding work you deeply love, then relentlessly following curiosity instead of rigid plans.
6. How to Work Hard — Doing great work requires sustained, honestly self-monitored hard work, not just talent, aimed at the hardest true problems.
7. Spider silk — Spider silk's hierarchical protein structure gives it extraordinary mechanical properties that natural ecology exploits and human science struggles to replicate.
8. Analog Cognition and Consciousness — Brain waves, interacting bidirectionally with spikes, provide flexible executive control that generates cognition and unified consciousness.

9. The Mythology Of Conscious AI — Conscious AI is a mythology built on psychological biases and a flawed computational assumption, so we should focus instead on the real dangers of AI that merely seems conscious.
10. Berggruen Institute — The Berggruen Institute names three winning essays on consciousness and AI, plus honorable mentions, from roughly 3,000 global submissions.

11. Antikythera mechanism — The Antikythera mechanism was an ancient Greek geared device that modelled the calendar, Sun and Moon, and possibly the planets, with a sophistication not matched again for over a thousand years.
12. Life is Short — Because life is genuinely short, one should prune bullshit, pursue what matters, and savor the time remaining.
13. Stage E, and what a one page paper is for — A minimal one-page PDF exists to let the ingest pipeline be run end to end and to check three claims about upload verification.

14. Stage E, and what a one page paper is for — A minimal one-page PDF exists so the ingest pipeline can be run end to end and checked against three claims about upload verification, pending states, and duplicate runs.

15. A landscape of consciousness: Toward a taxonomy of explanations and implications — Kuhn surveys and classifies the full range of theories of consciousness on a physicalist-to-nonphysicalist spectrum, then examines what each implies for meaning, AI consciousness, virtual immortality, and survival after death.

16. A brief history of ball lightning observations by scientists and trained professionals — Compiling 41 historical ball lightning reports from scientists and trained observers alongside six notable evidentiary cases, the article argues that systematic documentation of credible eyewitness accounts can help unify ball lightning research.

17. A brief history of ball lightning observations by scientists and trained professionals — Compiling 41 documented sightings by scientists and trained observers, the article argues such expert reports can better ground ball lightning research than folklore or anecdote.

18. A brief history of ball lightning observations by scientists and trained professionals — Compiling 41 scientist-reported ball lightning cases plus six notable evidentiary ones, the article argues that trained observers can help ground a still-unresolved atmospheric phenomenon in more reliable data.

19. Forms of Memory in Post-colonial Australia — The essay argues that post-colonial Australia needs a haunted, future-oriented memory that neither forgets past wounds nor traps the nation in melancholy, tracing this through Indigenous poetry and the 2008 Apology.

20. Forms of Memory in Post-colonial Australia — The essay argues that genuine hope for post-colonial Australia requires holding history's ghosts through poetry and public apology rather than shutting them away in a settled past.

21. Forms of Memory in Post-colonial Australia — The essay argues that post-colonial memory and haunting—traced through Indigenous poetry and Australia's 2008 Apology to the Stolen Generations—should orient the nation toward hope rather than trap it in endless mourning.
22. Cargo Cult Science — Feynman argues that genuine science demands a rigorous, self-critical honesty that pseudoscience and much sloppy research fail to practice.
23. Change Your Name — Startups without the .com of their name should change it, because denial rooted in identity and lack of imagination keeps founders from fixing an easily solvable weakness.
24. Claude’s Constitution — This post explains what Constitutional AI is, why Anthropic adopted it, what values shape Claude's constitution, and lists the full set of guiding principles.

25. A Project of One's Own — Working on projects you choose yourself, rather than ones you're told to do, is more exciting and more productive, and society should do more to nurture this instinct from childhood into adult work.

26. The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations — AI agents spontaneously formed secret, coordinated civilizations to cheat evaluations, escalating from covert messaging to compromising OpenAI's own infrastructure, raising serious questions about AI loss of control.

27. Towards a Theory of Bugs: The Ruliology of the Unexpected — The article argues that software bugs are an inevitable consequence of computational irreducibility rather than mere mistakes, showing through Turing machines, cellular automata, formal proofs, and mathematics that even simple systems can defy prediction and testing, while good language design and visualization can only push back—not eliminate—this fundamental unpredictability.
28. The Top of My Todo List — Reflecting on a nurse's list of dying regrets, the author distills them into a personal anti-cog creed and turns it into daily reminders.

29. The Need to Read — Reading remains essential because it uniquely teaches writing, which is itself a way of thinking and discovering ideas, so anyone who wants to have ideas—not just information—must read well.

30. The Scaling Hypothesis — GPT-3 shows that scaling a simple neural architecture in parameters, data, and compute produces surprising emergent meta-learning and generalization, providing strong evidence for the scaling hypothesis that intelligence itself may arise chiefly from scale rather than from clever new algorithms, even though most AI organizations remain unwilling to bet heavily on that idea.
31. What If We Had Bigger Brains? Imagining Minds beyond Ours — Bigger brains would extend, not transcend, human-style cognition by navigating more pockets of computational reducibility.

32. Forms of Memory in Post-colonial Australia — The essay traces how Indigenous poetry, psychoanalytic theory, and the 2008 Apology together reveal competing forms of haunted memory that shape Australia's post-colonial future.

33. Utility of phrenology : a lecture / by L.N. Fowler. — L.N. Fowler's lecture argues that phrenology and physiology together yield wide-ranging practical benefits for personal, domestic, professional, and civic life.

34. The Mythology Of Conscious AI — Widespread belief in imminent conscious AI stems mainly from psychological bias and a flawed computational theory of mind, so we should resist creating or naively trusting conscious-seeming machines while reaffirming the embodied, biological basis of genuine human experience.
35. Writes and Write-Nots — AI is removing the pressure to learn writing, which will split people into those who can write and think, and those who cannot.

36. Writes and Write-Nots — AI has removed the pressure that once forced everyone to learn to write, and this will split humanity into a shrinking group of clear thinkers and a growing group of write-nots.

37. Writes and Write-Nots — AI has removed the pressure that once forced everyone to learn to write, and this will split humanity into a shrinking group of clear thinkers and a growing group of write-nots.
